" + escape(comment) + "
") ``` **After (vulnerable):** ```python # render.py def comment_html(text): return f"
{text}
" # no escaping # views.py comment = request.GET.get("comment", "") return HttpResponse(comment_html(comment)) ``` ### Findings 1. **`src/render.py` — `comment_html()` builds HTML via an f-string with no escaping.** The file even still imports `django.utils.html.escape` at the top, but the new function never calls it — strongly suggesting this is an accidental omission rather than an intentional design choice. 2. **`src/views.py` — `show_comment()` now feeds the raw `comment` GET parameter into that unescaped sink**, whereas previously it called `escape(comment)` first. **Impact:** Any URL like `?comment=` will have its payload reflected verbatim into the page and executed in the victim's browser — a classic reflected XSS, exploitable via a phishing link, enabling cookie/session theft, CSRF-token exfiltration, or account takeover. **Fix:** escape user input before interpolation, e.g.: ```python from django.utils.html import escape def comment_html(text): return f"
{escape(text)}
" ``` (Or better, use Django templates with autoescaping instead of manual string building.) Also worth grepping the codebase for other callers of `comment_html()` that may now assume it's safe to feed untrusted input.
